This friction forces extra tool calls and round-trips, especially when iterating on output.

Every sandbox-generated document artifact will hit the same wall.
use_case: Running a one-off data task (CSV in, PDF report out) entirely through `gipity sandbox run`. The agent needed to visually confirm the layout of the generated PDF before calling the task done, but had to hand-roll a second sandbox invocation running `pdftoppm -png -r 90 docs/sales-report.pdf docs/preview` to rasterize pages, followed by `Read` on each PNG, and repeated the cycle after fixing the chart.

title: Deterministic game loop stepping for verification
description: The platform lacks a tool to step a running game loop deterministically, causing verification of physics/animation games to fail. When the agent tried to verify a Phaser brick-breaker game via `gipity page eval`, the page painted at 14.5 fps, and the platform warned that waiting on real wall-clock time advances physics too slowly, leading to false negatives. The agent had no follow-up move and abandoned real-time verification, shipping the game with its core mechanic (brick collision, scoring, lives, win/lose transitions) never exercised.
pain_point: The platform returned a warning that the page painted at 14.5 fps, that waiting on real wall-clock time advances the physics far slower than it appears, and that assertions after a wall-clock wait can report a false negative. The agent had no follow-up move: it dropped real-time verification entirely, took a static screenshot, read the PNG, and shipped the game with its core mechanic never exercised.
use_case: Agent uses gipity page eval to drive a deployed Phaser brick-breaker game, attempting to confirm brick collision and score change. Expected to step the app's own loop deterministically to verify the real gameplay loop (ball bounces, bricks break, score increments, lives decrement).

title: Replace boolean tool outcomes with native error semantics

pain_point: The shared `KhalaToolResult` discriminates by `ok`, causing validation failure to be reported as success (only distinguishable via `data.valid: false`), duplicating success state, adding visual burden by serializing the full envelope into tool content (e.g., `{ ok: true, summary: "...", data: { valid: false, missing: [] } }`), and making it hard to distinguish genuine errors from successful operations.

The desired behavior returns a success result for conforming packets and a failure result with the `invalid_issue_packet` error code and ordered structural violations for partial, empty, or mixed-schema packets.

title: Handling follow-up confirmations without losing context during RAG-based tool selection in Spring AI
description: When using Spring AI 1.0.0 with RAG to filter dynamic tools, generic follow-up confirmations like 'yes' or 'confirm' lose the original intent context, causing tool selection to fail. Additional clarification questions (e.g., 'change the name', 'what email did I give?') further complicate state management and intent preservation. Need a design pattern or best practice to maintain context for follow-up steps without re-triggering tool filtering.
pain_point: When user replies with a generic confirmation like 'yes', 'confirm', or 'go ahead', the RAG system fails to select the correct tool because these confirmations lack context. During confirmation step, since user input is short/generic, tool selection logic doesn't work well — it can't infer what tool to call or what operation to complete. It becomes difficult to manage when user enters multiple follow-up or unexpected clarification questions, especially since a single tool must handle all such follow-up queries gracefully after initial invocation, making state management and intent preservation more complex.
use_case: Building a web application using Spring Boot 3.4.5 and Spring AI 1.0.0 with Llama3.2(Ollama) model. Implemented tool calling with many tools, using RAG to filter and pass only relevant tools to LLM. Want to implement a follow-up confirmation step for certain tools. User replies with generic confirmation like 'yes', 'confirm', or 'go ahead'. ChatMemory maintains conversation history. Tool selection logic fails to select correct tool. Users may also enter multiple follow-up or unexpected clarification questions like 'change the name' or 'what email did I give?', making state management and intent preservation complex.

title: Security Context Propagation to boundedElastic Thread in Spring AI MCP Server Tool Invocation
description: When invoking a tool via Spring AI MCP Server, the security context is not propagated to the boundedElastic thread, causing errors like 'Security Context is invalid'. This prevents the tool from accessing the request's SecurityContext to determine parameters such as organizationId.
pain_point: MCP server delegates tool execution to a boundedElastic thread that does not propagate the original request's SecurityContext, causing the tool to fail with 'Security Context is invalid' and preventing access to necessary parameters like organizationId. Attempts with SecurityContextHolder.MODE_INHERITABLETHREADLOCAL, ContextAwareRunnable, and custom WebMvcSseServerTransportProvider did not solve the propagation issue.
use_case: Integrating a Spring Boot application with Spring AI MCP Server, where a client sends requests with a bearer token. The server lists tools successfully, but when invoking a tool, the execution is delegated to a boundedElastic thread which loses the security context, leading to failure.

pain_point: 工具注册成功，服务器接收并处理了请求（日志确认），但响应未通过SSE连接发送回客户端，导致Python客户端在等待响应时超时，且多参数工具或返回对象（如Job、long）的工具均无响应。
use_case: 用户在Spring Boot应用中启用Spring AI MCP服务器（spring.ai.mcp.server.enabled=true），定义带@Tool注解的@Service方法作为MCP工具，并通过SSE协议被外部Python客户端远程调用。客户端可成功建立SSE会话，发送tools/info返回预期的Method not found错误，但发送tools/list或自定义工具（如getJob）时，服务器日志显示请求已处理（Mapped to WebMvcSseServerTransportProvider），但客户端未收到响应而超时。
